prompt: Each case shows one way B2B markets differ from B2C markets. Which one is it?

cases.text: A jet engine maker sells to only a handful of aircraft makers, and each order is worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
cases.explanation: A few customers, each buying a lot: B2B markets typically have fewer, but much larger, buyers than B2C markets.

cases.text: A leather tannery gets fewer orders because shoppers are buying fewer handbags this year.
cases.explanation: The tannery's orders follow what shoppers buy. Its demand is derived demand, meaning it comes from consumer demand.

cases.text: A steel mill's orders jump by 40% one quarter and drop by 35% the next.
cases.explanation: Big swings from one quarter to the next show B2B demand fluctuating more rapidly than consumer demand.

cases.text: When more Montrealers take up cycling, a maker of bike chains gets more orders from bike makers.
cases.explanation: The chain maker sells to bike makers, but its orders rise because consumers want more bikes. That is derived demand.

cases.text: A tire maker sells to five car companies, while a sneaker brand sells to millions of runners.
cases.explanation: Five car companies against millions of runners: the B2B seller has fewer, but much larger, buyers.

cases.text: People buy about the same amount of cereal every week, yet the box maker's orders swing up and down from month to month.
cases.explanation: Steady consumer buying next to swinging orders for boxes: B2B demand fluctuates more rapidly than consumer demand.

prompt: Sort each purchase: does it show the traits of a B2B purchase or of a B2C purchase?

cards.text: Engineers, finance staff and a plant manager all sign off before a factory buys a new robot.
cards.explanation: Many people take part, so it has more decision participants, a trait of B2B purchases.

cards.text: A student grabs a sandwich between classes.
cards.explanation: One person decides in a moment, with no formal process: a consumer purchase.

cards.text: A hospital follows a written approval process with set steps before it buys an MRI machine.
cards.explanation: The B2B buying process is highly formalized, with written steps and approvals.

cards.text: A couple picks a sofa after a weekend of browsing stores.
cards.explanation: Two people shop for their own home. That is a consumer purchase, not an organization's formal buying effort.

cards.text: An airline and its engine supplier work together for decades, and neither could easily replace the other.
cards.explanation: Buyers and sellers are highly dependent on each other in B2B markets and build long term relationships.

cards.text: A shopper switches coffee brands because another one is on sale this week.
cards.explanation: No close tie to the seller and no formal process: a quick consumer choice.

prompt: A restaurant chain is buying new kitchen ovens. Which buying center role does each person play?

cases.text: Lina is a line cook who will bake with the new ovens every shift.
cases.explanation: Users are members of the organization who will actually use the product.

cases.text: An engineer writes down the size, power and heat the ovens must have.
cases.explanation: Influencers affect the buying decision by providing information or specifications.

cases.text: The purchasing manager picks the oven supplier and negotiates the price and delivery dates.
cases.explanation: Buyers have formal authority to select the supplier and arrange terms.

cases.text: An outside energy consultant sends a report comparing how much power each oven uses.
cases.explanation: The consultant provides information that shapes the decision, which is what influencers do.

cases.text: The pastry team will run the ovens every morning to bake bread.
cases.explanation: They will actually use the product, so they are users.

cases.text: Marc from procurement signs the purchase contract with the chosen supplier.
cases.explanation: Arranging the terms with the supplier is the buyer's formal authority.

prompt: Each case is a business purchase. Which buying situation is it?

cases.text: An office reorders the same printer paper from the same supplier, as it does every month.
cases.explanation: A routine reorder without modifications is a straight rebuy.

cases.text: A café chain keeps its cup supplier but now wants compostable cups at a new price.
cases.explanation: The buyer wants to modify product specifications and prices, so it is a modified rebuy.

cases.text: A farm buys crop-spraying drones for the first time.
cases.explanation: The buyer purchases the product for the first time, so it is a new task.

cases.text: A school board keeps buying the same laptops but moves the order to a cheaper supplier.
cases.explanation: Changing the supplier is a modification, so this is a modified rebuy.

cases.text: A clinic's system automatically reorders the same box of gloves whenever stock runs low.
cases.explanation: Nothing changes in the order, so it is a straight rebuy.

cases.text: A small firm buys accounting software for the first time after years of spreadsheets.
cases.explanation: It has never bought this kind of product before, so it is a new task.

question_text: A packaging firm earns most of its profit from three large retailers, so it gives each one a dedicated team and custom solutions. What is the firm practicing?
hint: Look for the most valuable customers, dedicated teams, and customized solutions.

options.option_text: A straight rebuy, since the retailers reorder the same packaging.
options.option_explanation: A straight rebuy describes a buyer's routine reorder, not how a supplier manages its most valuable customers.

options.option_text: Derived demand, since retailers set the firm's prices.
options.option_explanation: Derived demand is about demand coming from consumer demand. This case is about dedicated teams for the top customers.

options.option_text: Gatekeeping, since the dedicated teams control information.
options.option_explanation: Gatekeepers control the flow of information inside a buying organization, not a supplier's service to its best customers.

options.option_text: Key Account Management with its most valuable customers.
options.option_explanation: Correct. KAM builds long term relationships with the most valuable customers, who contribute disproportionately to revenue and profit, through dedicated teams and customized solutions.
